sentences.text: The known fossil material includes the rear part of a skull, disarticulated teeth, the first cervical vertebra, and two armor plates.
The genus name combines the Japanese word for Japan with the Greek word for shield.
The species name refers to Yezo, the traditional name for Hokkaido, the location of the discovery.
The holotype specimen of Nipponopelta was discovered by Eijiro Goto on June 25, 1995, in Yūbari, Hokkaido, Japan.
The fossil was found inside a calcareous concretion that had eroded from the Hikagenosawa Formation.
The fossil was donated to the Mikasa City Museum and accessioned as specimen MCM A522.
Nipponopelta was formally described as a new genus and species in 2026 by Shumpei Oyabu and colleagues, with MCM A522 designated as the holotype.
Researchers suggest that Nipponopelta likely inhabited near-marine environments such as coastal and estuarine areas.
Scientists note that the presence of nodosaurid fossils in marine deposits might be partly due to the transport of carcasses after death.
Nipponopelta is classified as a member of the family Nodosauridae.
Phylogenetic analysis places Nipponopelta within the Nodosaurinae subfamily, closer to Nodosaurus and Panoplosaurus than to Polacanthus or Struthiosaurus.
Nipponopelta lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically the Cenomanian age.
The estimated time range for Nipponopelta is between 100.5 and 93.9 million years ago.
The genus is known from the Upper Cretaceous Hikagenosawa Formation of the Yezo Group in Japan.
It is debated whether nodosaurid fossils found in marine deposits represent the actual habitat of the animals or result from post-mortem transport.
